This function now only handles saving the new asset info into the data (thumbnail path if available) and then putting a job into the `asset-uploaded` queue. The first stage in the diagram.

![immich-queue-layour copy](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/27055614/172532372-f555e953-2b50-4245-91ab-450f728edce7.png)

This is the starting point of the microservice that handles post-upload-related tasks. It will then put the additional jobs into the corresponding queues.

* Generate JPEG Thumbnail
* Generate Webp Thumbnail <-> if JPEG thumbnail exists
* EXIF extractor
* Reverse Geocoding
* Video Encoding

I have a question regarding the handling of websockets: where is the WS connection used?

I'm asking because for what I've read online it's not possible to apply AuthGuards to the handleConnection() but only on the functions that handle specific messages. Since the verification of the JWT token is done by the already implemented strategies, it wouldn't be the nicest thing to rewrite the implementation of the token validation from scratch.

Hi, I'd like your opinion on the implementation of the authentication for the WebSocket.

As of today (and it's been like that for 3 years, see [this](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/issues/882)), NestJS doesn't allow to add AuthGuards to the handling of the connection.

So there is the (in my opinion) ugly solution which consists of reimplementing the same logic of the current Strategies (JWT verification with the secret key, expiration check and audience validation) and using that for the authentication during the initial phase of the websocket. That wouldn't be clean simply because of the code duplication.

The less ugly idea I found on the internet is to create an API calls that generates a ticket to be used only for one WS connection, during the `handleConnection()` the server verifies the presence of that token in the auth bearer and let the connection live if valid. This way the real authentication is handled by the HTTP call as all the other API calls, and the code would have way less bugs.

What do you think about this?

What I was thinking is using a one-time token. 
The client asks the server to generate the token, then the client uses that token on the first message to establish a new WS connection. The server checks the validity of that token and accept the connection, the used token is invalidated as a consequence. This way the token can be used only once, if the user want to create a new connection it has to ask for a new token.

Yes exactly, it's called definite assignment assertion. In general we should only be using these in Entities where properties are not null, because TypeORM cannot use a constructor to initialise the values. So we know that after the Entity is "hydrated" by TypeORM, those properties would have its value.

It doesn't, I just removed it because in these case is not useful. When using await what it does is, it resolves the promise, so we now have the "album entity", then it wraps it in another resolved promise which is then returned.

Without the await it just returns the promise. A good practice is to have the return values defined in the function (don't let TypeScript infer), in this case `Promise<AlbumEntity>`, so whatever you do inside you must still return that type or TypeScript will complain.

The entity has defined `albumThumbnailAssetId` as `nullable: true`. So when TypeORM "hydrated" the entity, it would set it to `null` or `string`. This spec was not setting `albumThumbnailAssetId` to anything (`undefined`), so the type was not matching what TypeORM would "hydrate" it to, and TypeScript was complaining because I used `undefined` (instead of null) later in one of the tests for checking the expectation.

finally figured out what's causing the different behavior (background service vs in foreground app):
The background process is started by the Android WorkManager and executes the new Java/Kotlin `BackupWorker`. This starts the Dart/Flutter runtime in a new thread. I Had to make the worker aware of running another async thread by not immediately stopping after finishing the code on the Java/Kotlin side. Instead a `ResolvableFuture` is used to tell the Android system that the process completed (successfully or failed). This signal is send by the dart/flutter thread once it finishes executing (i.e. `return Future.value(true);` in `callbackDispatcher` method handler). If the executed dart code calls an `async` function without `await` this function is executed in yet another thread and the main dart code continues, finished, and in turn signals Android that the background work is finished. The Android system then kills the entire process. Yet, this non-main async dart function (e.g. `backupAsset`) was still running and is killed along with its process.

tl;dr: all `async` functions need to be awaited else the thread/process is killed while executing them in the background.

Not await an async function is also a problem in the foreground app: If an error occurs in that function, it is silently ignored!

Whether to disable the service once the app is opened is good question. This is mostly a concurrency issue. What we must prevent is that the background service is uploading something, user opens the app and the foreground app also performs an upload (of potentially the same files). There are multiple options to consider:

1. When user opens the app: Stop the service (and kill any currently happening uploads), wait until stopped, check which assets to backup and perform upload as usual in the foreground app. Start service once app is closed ("inactive" / "paused"  state)
2. Remove foreground backup/upload (on Android) in the app entirely
3. Let the user decide whether to use either only foreground upload or use only the background service

Of these options, I think 2. is cleanest (and simplest), 1. is very difficult to get right and potentially wasteful regarding battery as uploads might be canceled and performed twice, 3. is nice as a safeguard if the background upload has issues (so manual foreground upload still works as is) and difficulty is somewhere between the other two options

> It that the mechanism "baked" into the background service implementation on the native side, such that when the app is in foreground, the background service would pause or stop running?

There is no automatic stopping (or pausing) of the background service. It runs entirely independent of the app.

It allows to get a copy that is actually safe to modify without changing the global state of `HiveBackupAlbums`.

Hive does not work like it's API indicates that it works. When you do:

1.  `info = box.get(backupInfoKey);`
2.  modify a few entries in `info`
3. ignore `info` and do nothing with it anymore
4. in some other method load `otherInfo = Hive.box<HiveBackupAlbums>(hiveBackupInfoBox).get(backupInfoKey)`

You would expect `info != otherInfo`. However, the changes made to `info` in 2. are also visible in `otherInfo` although it was not saved/put back into the box! This was a very painful and long debugging session.....

To guard against this, a deep copy of the arrays in `HiveBackupAlbums` is required.

The idea is the following:

When the user opens the app and the cached state is invalid, no assets are shown until `getAllAsset` completes and updates the state, In case the background service is running, this means that the user will not see any assets for minutes (frustrated, killing the app etc., reporting an issue..).
To guard against this, `urgent` can be set to true when the cached state is invalid. This activates a timeout when reading local assets. If it takes too long for the background service to finish, only remote assets are loaded and shown to the user (until the background service finishes and some action reloads the assets)

It allows to fetch remote and local assets concurrently.

If we put an `await` on line `35`, it would do this sequentially (and thus take longer in total)

Originally the repository was designed to be responsible for doing any work in the Entities (updating or creating). When an entity is returned from the repository it shouldn't be mutated by the services, and the services shouldn't create Entities.

- For create we pass in the createDto and the repository uses it to do an insert in the DB and returns an entity (since we are using ORM it actually creates a new Entity object and uses it to insert it. Then it returns a new created Entity)
- For update we pass in the entity that we got from a get (without mutating) and the UpdateDto. Then the repository updates it in the DB (since we are using ORM it actually merges the DTO into the Entity)

```typescript
Repository<UserEntity>.save<Partial<UserEntity>>(entity: Partial<UserEntity>, options?: SaveOptions | undefined): Promise<Partial<UserEntity> & UserEntity> 
```

Can you help me understand why we need this for our use case? I read the docs but didn't understand them very well. https://svelte.dev/tutorial/context-api

Other solutions are possible, but using context seemed best suited. You can use props, but then you have to pass the map to every component with something like:

```svelte
<Map bind:map={map}>
  <TileLayer {map} />
  <Marker {map} />
</Map>
```

That isn't needed with contexts. You set the `map` context once in the `Map` component and all children can access it. This is better manageable, especially when adding more components or even adding more contexts.

You can also use a store, but if you have two maps on one page, they would both interact with the same store leading to all sorts of issues. This doesn't happen with contexts, because they are limited to a single instance of a component.

There are two strategies I have seen.
1. Have a method that loads the entire object and use that method everywhere
2. Have specialized methods that load minimal data and use each one in one place.

We used to use TypeORM and option (1) everywhere. The result was a lot of overhead and inefficiency. We've been transitioning to option (2) instead. A lot of our jobs used to load a lot of data that they never used. Those types of queries have been replaced with specialized/minimal ones, which you can see in the `AssetJobRepository`.

I think it's more efficient, faster, and less memory intensive to use a specialized query and only load the info you need in order to do the required checks in this method. For me, I see no reason to load every asset in the stack, which technically could include like 1,000+ assets (since I don't believe we have any limitation on this). Especially if all you need is two booleans (is the asset in the stack, is the asset the stack primary)

A few reasons: 
1) This is to avoid permissions issues between the view of the files inside the container vs the ones on the bind-mount on the host. If the container were to be run by a user other than the user that owns the root of the git-clone on the host, then the files would be created with the owner of the user running the container, and if that happened to be 'root' then the files can't be cleaned up with a simple `make clean` command - it would require `sudo make clean` which is a little more dangerous/annoying. 
2) Isolation: All of dependency/package install commands are performed from within a docker container, which may be a different architecture (MacOS on arm) or libc (the web container uses alpine with *musl* instead of *glibc*) - and some of the dependent packages use native binary code, which only make sense in the architecture/libc version that is within the container it was executed inside. By using volumes, these dependencies are not created on the hosts filesystem. 
2) pnpm performs performs a clone, hard-link, or copy of files (in that order) from the content-addressable-store (`/buildcache/pnpm-store`) to the virtual store (`.pnpm-store`). And then creates the dependency node structures in `node_modules` using symlinks. Using volume mounts makes it more likely that hardlinks will be successful, increasing speed to install dependencies. 

oh, and named volumes vs anonymous volumes because anonymous volumes are removed when container is removed, and containers are auto-removed at the end of every `make` command.

Note: package.json still exists in each of the 8 workspace modules contained in this monorepo. 

However, reading it like this: 
```
const { version } = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./package.json', 'utf8'));
``` 
uses a relative path, which is resolved against the current-working-directory, which isn't `/usr/src/app/server` any longer. The way to fix this is read the file from the absolute path of the server package.json. This is determined by using the CommonJS style `__filename` global, mostly because the ESM alternative is more verbose, and -- well, the default output of the server is CommonJS anyways, not ESM, so using `import.meta.url` would end up requiring even more steps to adapt back to CommonJS.
No - the format of the the paths of individual dependencies served from `node_modules` when running in dev mode has changed, and this adapts the regexps to the pnpm's changes to these paths.

Its ok, this was found through very in-depth debugging. The point is that any javascript-triggered DOM scrolls (i.e. scrollTo/By/etc) will eventually call the DOM callback function `onScroll()` -- which `updateSlidingWindow()` is also invoked from. Normally, we would 'optimize' this routine, and just allow the callback function to call `updateSlidingWindow()`. However, there may be some time-delay, between the time the dom is 'requested to be scrolled' and the 'callbacks that are sent when it WAS actually scrolled'. If this time delay is long enough, other code (like svelte reactivity changes) may start to run. And this may cause the `monthGroup`'s intersecting flags to (very briefly, but OS/CPU dependent - but always, if your CPU is fast enough) be incorrect (since its referring to the pre-scroll positions, which are updated in the `updateSlidingWindow()` function) -- if this happens, the DOMs are destroyed and recreated very soon after - which is devastating for performance. 

So basically, if your computer is just slow enough, it triggers a downward performance spiral. 

Whats sorta interesting, is that after calling the explicit DOM scrollTo/By/etc functions, if we read the scroll position from the DOM - we get the actual current value. So, then, if we just manually call updateSlidingWindow() right after (which will update the intersections of all the months with the NEW values) everything syncs back up. 

This "deferred" scroll position and intersection support is pretty tricky to handle, since scrolls may trigger loads/unloads of months, which may change the size of the scrollable area, which also need to be adjusted (i.e. scrollCompensation --- but thats another story)

Considering `IN()` vs `= ANY(ARRAY)`.
On the one hand, code with `IN()` is concise and more readable than `= ANY(ARRAY)`.
On the other hand, two concerns:
- Bad reputation of `IN()` due to poor performance with large number of parameters in earlier Postgres versions. This is fixed since PG v14, so `IN()` performance is on par with `ANY()`.
- Max number of parameters in `IN()`. 65K is a hard cap from https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html. I tested rather low numbers, up to 3000 args, in the shell script (hitting OS limit of max arg length). With `ANY(ARRAY)` it would pass the entire array as a single parameter, thus avoiding the limit, in theory.

`unshift` and `reverse` run in O(n), `push` runs in O(1). So as it is, we keep linear time (n pushes => O(n) + reverse in O(n) => "O(2n)"), while unshift would result in n * O(n) => quadratic.

The shift-tab key binding is not observable in browsers. Browsers do not send the shift-tab keyDown combination to javascript code -- which meant that the current focus-trap implementation was not working properly. This was not detected by the test, because the shift-tab unit test had a typo in it. 

The common solution to this problem used by other focus trap libraries is to insert two "marker elements" - one at the beginning of the trap and one at the end - I'm naming these sentinel nodes, because there job is to listen/watch to the 'focus' event (instead of shift-tab). 

When the startSentinel element gets focus, it will set focus to the last focusable element. When the lastSentinel element gets focus, it will set focus to the first focusable element, thereby completing the trap.

In the case that there are no focusable elements, a backupSentinel element is inserted - the sole purpose of this element is to accept focus when there are no other elements available to focus. This is useful when, a modal without any input fields is open, but you still want to prevent focus from leaving the modal until it is dismissed.

The return type here is something that I made optional in #24056. In general, this is a violation of the (LoD) Law of Demeter. You should not ask the timeline what is being filtered, and then tell it to remove something based on that filter. Rather, you just tell it what the current state of something is (the visibility in this case) and it will figure it out on its own if it should be removed from the timeline or not.

This may vary based on the page the timeline is one (archive page, album page, favorites). The action would need to have special coding for each of those scenarios. If you just tell the timeline what the state should be, it can do it - and then the action doesn't need to have any special understanding of what to do, leading to a clearer API. 

So in general, {remove: false} is redundant. It should be the normal behavior. In fact, most clients don't ever need it - unless they are doing a specialized form of bulk-removal. Most of the time this can be accomplished with the `removeAssets(id[])` function

> Transparent image
> If only a single [Image](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-ui/Image-class.html) or [Color](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-ui/Color-class.html) needs to be composited with an opacity between 0.0 and 1.0, it's much faster to directly use them without [Opacity](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/widgets/Opacity-class.html) widgets.
> 
> For example, Container(color: Color.fromRGBO(255, 0, 0, 0.5)) is much faster than Opacity(opacity: 0.5, child: Container(color: Colors.red)).
> 
> 
> The following example draws an [Image](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-ui/Image-class.html) with 0.5 opacity without using [Opacity](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/widgets/Opacity-class.html):
> [link](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/#)
> content_copy
> Image.network(

Before it was assigning `data.user`. I meant the derived `user` object

The `data` returned by a load function is read-only, you can’t update it by reassigning it, you can only get fresh values by invalidating and re-running the load function.

1. Opening the edit modal navigates to `/[id]/edit`, and the modal reads the user from the layout’s load data
2. After saving, you’re redirected back to `/[id]`, and the local user state updates correctly there
3. When you open the edit modal again, it still reads the layout's load data, which hasn’t been re-run, so it shows the old (stale) values

To fix step 3, we need to invalidate so it re-fetches and the edit modal always gets the latest user data.

Since classes are limited in expressing complex union types (implemented with e.g. `zod.coerce`), they don't work on all schemas. nestjs-zod emits separate "_Output" component schemas for response types
(via z.toJSONSchema's "output" IO mode). This is correct when input/output
shapes genuinely differ (e.g. coercion, transforms, codecs), but for most
schemas (especially enums) input and output are identical, producing
redundant schemas that cause client generators to emit duplicate models
(e.g. ReactionType + ReactionType_Output, ActivityResponseDto + ActivityResponseDto_Output).

Collapse "_Output" variants that are identical to their base schema, and
rename orphaned "_Output" schemas (where no base exists) to keep generated
client model names stable and free of unnecessary duplication.

**This openapi patch is necessary, as it prevents model duplication, response type unions, and structural divergences that could break existing client code across clients (TS, Python, Dart)**

`nestjs-zod` generates `_Output` types because it treats Zod schemas as potentially having different input and output shapes, even when we already separate request and response DTOs.

It does this because Zod schemas can have different input vs output types due to:
- `.transform()` 
- `.preprocess()`
- `.coerce.*`
- `.default()` (affects required/optional)
- Codecs (encode vs decode)

So it generates both variants to be safe, even if the schema doesn't use any of these features.

I looked into converting this to $effect and it doesn't work cleanly here. The core issue is timing: $derived.by evaluates synchronously before the template renders, so adaptiveImageLoader is always available. $effect runs after the render cycle, which means the loader would be undefined for the first frame (and on every asset change).

This matters because `adaptiveImageLoader` in the template. Converting to $effect would require `?.` null guards at **~20** places. So, the code becomes less readable (IMHO)

The $derived.by + untrack() pattern here is basically memoization: "if asset/sharedLink haven't changed, return the cached loader; otherwise create a new one." The other "state"" is really just the previous generation of the same loader. The mutations inside `untrack()` are specifically to maintain that memoization without creating circular reactivity.

Destroyed is only set when the component is destroyed. It prevent the onLoad() from triggering after the component has been unmounted/destroyed. (The browser still sends these events even though there the object is not in the DOM)

AdaptiveImage sets `src` initially to bound/state variable that is initially undefined - If you add an image with a undefined `src` to the DOM it shows up as a broken image. When its time to load an image, the bound variable is set to a string. This causes the `img` to be mounted to DOM, runs the `onStart()`, `onLoad()`, and `onError()` (if errored) handlers. The `#key` block ensures that the `` is always recreated if the `src` changes. The key block is important because if you change the `src` of an image after it is already in the dom, it will not progressively decode like it does the first time. It effectively behaves as `` - which is exactly the opposite of what the `` needs. The other destroy guards, returns as part of the `$effect`, are there so that if the element is removed from dom, or canceled (which presents itself as an error) - that the (now stale) callbacks are not invoked.

Unfortunately, running as a non-node user makes it really hard to inherit the docker compose files that do not run as node. There has always been issues with permissions in the dev containers. i.e. if you start clean - never run `pnpm install` and do a `make dev` the `pnpm install` will occur within the containers, which are bind-mounted to the host. a lot of the node-modules directories are volumes, but - the actual node_module directory on the host that is the target of the bind mount is created by the user that runs the container, in this case root. Likewise, the `dist` and `output` folders of all the projects are not volumes, so they will also be with root permission. The easiest way to resolve this is to either `sudo make clean` to delete them, or - run `pnpm i` and `make setup-web-dev` on the HOST. this will create those directories on the host using your current user, and when the docker container starts, it will preserve ownership - most of the time. Its definitely not perfect. However, without moving the dev containers and the production containers to a `rootless` user by default, I don't see a practical solution.

I believe this is in line with what was asked. The way media.service gets a buffer is via decodeImage. A bit confusing, both media.service and media.repository have a function called decodeImage. The other place that calls .metadata() is getImageDimensions() in media.service - but this isn't ever called on the source image - it is called on the extracted preview image from raw images with embedded previews. An earlier comment noted to add/piggyback the hasAlpha onto the getImageDimensions function, and rename getImageDimensions to be getMetadata(), which won't work here. 

So, instead, I put the call to `.metadata()` within decodeImage directly. It could be made into its own method, but it would only be used by decodeImage here. This method uses the pre-existing pipeline (sharp instance) - vs how getImageDimensions() does it (by creating a new sharp instance). 

In testing the performance - a sharp instance is really lightweight - I suppose we don't need to share the sharp instance from decodeImage. 

However, .metadata() will not work on a decoded image - since .metadata() is not preserved once an image has been decoded. You CAN get the channels from the decoded image (1,2,3,4) where 2= alpha+gray, and 4=CYMK or RGBA. But, since you can't tell if its CYMK or RGBA from the decoded image, we need the original source to be 100% reliable. We can't even use the source's file type to determine this confidently, because some image types (tiff and jxl) support both CYMK and RGBA formats. 

Additionally, in perf testing, calling .metadata() on a raw file is really really bad. It re-read the ENTIRE raw file to get .metadata(), unlike every other file-type, where .metadata() doesn't rely on decoding the image, and just looked at file headers. 

So, the best thing to do is to avoid calling .metadata() on raw images (hence the canHaveAlpha functions) - and to do the .metadata() on the original source image. 

With all that being said - if there is a strong desire to split out the .metadata() to its own function (outside of decodeImage) that can probably be done without a perf cost, since sharp instances are light, and metadata() doesn't really decode the image data (so doesn't need to be part of a pipeline)

Using the full asset as the key forces a full teardown when **any** property changes (e.g. `isFavorite`), which is what causes the video player to restart and the freeze/MissingPluginException. I can think of two ways to handle both issues.

In the `from21To22` migration, `newColumns: [column]` and `columnTransformer: {column: ...}` are both set for the same column in each `TableMigration`. In Drift's `TableMigration`, `newColumns` is intended for columns that are added fresh (not present in the old table), while `columnTransformer` is used to supply the value expression for a renamed or transformed column.

Including `newColumns: [column]` here is redundant because `duration_in_milliseconds` is not actually a genuinely new column — it replaces the old `duration_in_seconds` column via rename-and-transform. Drift handles this via `columnTransformer` alone. The `newColumns` entry causes Drift to also issue an `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` statement before building the migration, which adds overhead and could be confusing. The `newColumns` list should be removed from each `TableMigration` call, leaving only the `columnTransformer`.

saveToFilesLegacy() blocks waiting up to 5 seconds for MediaScannerConnection.scanFile() via CountDownLatch.await. Besides being susceptible to ANRs if still on the main thread, this can also return null on timeout even though the file was successfully written (making the Dart side treat the save as failed). Consider making the scan fully async (or running the wait off the UI thread) and providing a deterministic success signal (e.g., returning a file/MediaStore Uri fallback when scanning times out).

The docstring for mimeTypeForFile() says it "maps known unsupported extensions" (plural), but the implementation currently only special-cases CR3 and returns the wildcard for everything else. Either narrow the wording to match the current behavior or extend the mapping if additional types are intended to be supported here.

RawFileSaverPlugin performs potentially heavy disk I/O (FileInputStream.copyTo, MediaScannerConnection + CountDownLatch.await) directly inside the MethodChannel handler call path. MethodChannel handlers run on the Android main thread by default, so this can freeze the UI and risk ANRs when saving large RAW files. Move the save/scanning work onto a background thread (e.g., coroutines with Dispatchers.IO) and only call result.success/error back on the main thread once complete.

In saveToDownloads(), resolver.openOutputStream(uri) can return null. The current code silently skips writing but still clears IS_PENDING, which can leave a 0-byte entry in Downloads. Treat a null OutputStream as an error (delete the inserted row and return/throw) so callers don't get a false success and no corrupt placeholder file is left behind.

The `saveImageWithFile` path for CR3 on Android passes the unvalidated `title` value (derived from server-controlled `asset.originalFileName`) to `_saveRawFileOnAndroid`, which forwards it as the `title` argument over the `immich/raw_file_saver` channel. On pre-Android Q devices, the native `RawFileSaverPlugin.saveToFilesLegacy` implementation uses this `title` directly in `File(destDir, title)`, so an attacker who uploads an asset with a filename containing path separators or `..` can cause the app to write CR3 files outside the intended `DCIM/Immich` directory or overwrite arbitrary files on external storage. Sanitize and normalize `title` on the Dart side before invoking the native channel (e.g., enforce a basename-only filename without path segments) so the native plugin cannot be driven into path traversal by untrusted remote filenames.

Its slightly problematic to parse out all the domains from a mapbox json. It can contain 'sources' that have 'urls' that fetch other domains. i.e. for immich, this is where 'static.immich.cloud' comes from - in addition to the tiles.immich.cloud for the main .json file. 

An easy and reliable way to solve this problem is to not have the browser directly contact the map server. Instead, create a rest endpoint on the api server itself to proxy the tile requests. This way, the browser CSP does not need to carve out an exception - as all requests will go back to the same server (`self:`). 

Downsides: 
* May add some latency - uses your servers upstream bandwidth. 

Upsides: 
* potentially have the server do some caching
* you increase some privacy - the map server only sees the ip address of the server, not every browser/mobile device your using. 

In general, having every 3rd party request go through the api server would be my preferred solution - mostly for privacy - and for observability - knowing that I (as an admin) am in control all all URLs the browser touches.

1. RAF in general requires you to handle 'dropped frames' - which keeps it fast. Basically, its time-based instead of frame-based. RAF gives you a timestamp, and you figure out how far along you should be (interpolated), and then return the state of the animation at time `T`.

Do we really need this check? Elements are only added to the DOM if they're visible or near visible already?

This check skips the thumbhash fade-out. Elements are only added to the DOM when they are within +/- 500px of the viewport (intersecting) or in the viewport itself. actuallyIntersecting means the element is actually IN the viewport. So when !actuallyIntersecting is true at load time, the thumbnail loaded within the offscreen margins. In that case, we skip the thumbhash fade-out — the placeholder is instantly hidden.

Before this change, the 100ms fade-out would play offscreen, and would almost always complete before the element scrolled into view. This change eliminates the edge case where fast scrolling (>500px/100ms) could cause you to see a partial thumbhash fade-out on an element that loaded in the margins.

5000px/s is fast but achievable. In practice, any partial fade at these scroll speeds would be too brief to notice — but this change eliminates it entirely.

`HttpClientManager.rebuildCronetEngine()` is executed outside of `runCatching`, so if rebuilding throws (e.g., cache path still locked / "Disk cache storage path already in use"), the coroutine will abort before `draining` is reset and before `onCacheCleared` is invoked. That can leave the fetcher permanently stuck in `draining=true` and the caller waiting indefinitely. Consider wrapping the rebuild + callback in a `try/finally` that always clears `draining`, and include rebuild failures in the `Result` passed to `onCacheCleared`.

`rebuildCronetEngine()` now overwrites `cronetEngine` without shutting down the previous instance. If this method is called without an explicit `cronetEngine.shutdown()` beforehand, the old engine can remain alive (keeping the disk cache path locked and leaking resources). Consider making `rebuildCronetEngine()` responsible for shutting down/replacing atomically (e.g., capture current engine, set `cronetEngine` to the new instance, then shutdown the old one) or rename the method to reflect that callers must manage shutdown.

`_cacheListener` can be reassigned after it becomes `null` (e.g., when the cache listener is removed due to `ImageCache.clear()` or the initial-image sync attach/detach). In that case the next *UI* listener can be incorrectly treated as the cache listener, and `onlyCacheListenerLeft` may cancel the request while a real UI listener is still attached (e.g., two widgets share the same image, one detaches leaving the remaining widget misidentified as cache). Consider tracking “cache listener has been identified once” separately and never reassigning `_cacheListener` after the first attachment (even if it later becomes null).

The “ignore first sync removal” logic currently ignores the first `removeListener` call unconditionally when `hadInitialImage` is true, regardless of which listener is being removed, and after already decrementing `_listenerCount` and possibly nulling `_cacheListener`. This can swallow a legitimate last-listener removal (leaving the underlying request running with no listeners) and it also contributes to `_cacheListener` being lost/reassigned. Restrict this ignore to the specific synchronous cache-listener detach case (e.g., `listener == _cacheListener` and the removal happens immediately after a sync `setImage`), and avoid mutating tracking state in a way that makes later listeners look like cache.

`onCacheCleared` is nulled out before the async shutdown/delete work completes. If `clearCache()` is called again while `draining` is still true, it can set a new `onCacheCleared` but `drain()` will early-return (already draining) and the callback will never be invoked. Consider keeping `onCacheCleared` set until the coroutine finishes (or explicitly rejecting/queuing subsequent clearCache calls while draining) so callbacks can’t be lost.

`HttpClientManager.swapCronetEngine()` is called outside `runCatching`. If it throws (e.g., Cronet build failure), this coroutine will be cancelled and `draining` won’t be reset and `onCacheCleared` won’t be called. Wrap the whole operation in `try/finally` (or `runCatching`) to guarantee `draining = false` and callback invocation on all failure paths.

`cronetDirIndex` is read directly from SharedPreferences and used in the directory name. If the stored value is corrupted or from a future/older build, this can create unexpected directories (including negative indices) and break the intended “two directories” toggle. Consider normalizing/clamping the loaded value to 0/1 before using it to form the path.
```suggestion
      val storedCronetDirIndex = prefs.getInt(PREFS_CRONET_DIR_INDEX, 0)
      cronetDirIndex = if (storedCronetDirIndex <= 0) 0 else 1
```

`swapCronetEngine()` holds `synchronized(this)` while calling `buildCronetEngine()`, which can be relatively expensive/blocking. This increases the chance of lock contention with other synchronized methods on `HttpClientManager` (e.g., header/cert updates) and can stall callers. Consider restructuring so the expensive engine build happens outside the synchronized block (e.g., compute the new dir/index under lock, build the engine without the lock using an explicit storage path parameter, then swap fields under lock).
